chapter_theme: Rain is the unacknowledged condition of everything: food, farming, the sea's life, worship, giving, austerity and conduct. The chapter makes virtue and the gods depend on a natural cause.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: rain as the cause of the world's going on (11-17), and as the cause of virtue, wealth and pleasure (18-20).

11.reading: Because the world keeps going through the rain's constancy, rain deserves to be understood as amrita.
11.nuance: The word உணரற்பாற்று makes this a matter of recognition, since rain is ordinary and easily taken for granted. Manakkudavar draws this out by saying it should not be thought of as a mere element.

12.reading: Rain produces the food that eaters eat, and rain is itself food to those who drink it.
12.nuance: Five uses of துப்பு pack the couplet, and the wordplay enacts the idea: the same substance is the maker, the made and the eater's need.

13.reading: If the sky fails, hunger stays and torments this wide world, though it is surrounded by spreading water.
13.nuance: The irony is in விரிநீர்: the world is ringed by water and still starves. Parimelazhagar makes this explicit. பொய்ப்பின் also treats the sky as something that can break its word.

14.reading: If the bounty of the rains declines, ploughmen will not plough.
14.nuance: Parimelazhagar takes the verse as explaining why food runs out. The human labour is real but placed downstream of a yield the farmer doesn't control.

15.reading: Rain is what ruins, and then it is rain again that supports and lifts up the ruined.
15.nuance: The verse says only that rain ruins. The commentators here take the ruin as failure to fall, though a reader might expect flood too. The power to destroy and restore belongs to one impersonal agent, with no moral reason given.

16.reading: Unless drops fall from the sky, it is hard to see even the head of a green blade of grass.
16.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the implied 'even': if the grass is gone, not even a life with one sense remains. The argument descends to the smallest thing that lives.

17.reading: Even the vast sea would lose its nature if the cloud held back after taking from it.
17.nuance: The source of rain needs rain, so the dependence runs in a circle. Parimelazhagar makes this the point, and Kalaignar turns the same cycle into a social lesson.

positions.position: தடிந்து means the cloud scoops up the sea's water, and the sea's 'nature' is its living creatures and gems.
He takes the word as the cloud flashing, and reports that others read it as dividing.
The verse also teaches that those who rise from a society must serve it for it to live.
positions.quote: மனித சமுதாயத்திலிருந்து புகழுடன் உயர்ந்தவர்களும் அந்தச் சமுதாயத்திற்கே பயன்பட்டால்தான் அந்தச் சமுதாயம் வாழும்.

18.reading: If the sky dries up, festival and worship will cease here, even for the gods.
18.nuance: The word 'even' reverses the usual order: the celestials depend on what the sky provides through human offering. Kalaignar's comment adds scepticism with 'those said to live in the sky', which the verse does not express.

19.reading: If the sky does not give, neither giving nor austerity will last in this wide world.
19.nuance: Parimelazhagar maps giving broadly to the householder and austerity to the renunciant, so this verse quietly announces the two paths that chapters 3 and 5 go on to compare. Even austerity, which might seem independent of plenty, is included.

20.reading: If no one's world can do without water, then its flow can't exist without the sky.
20.nuance: The whole dispute rests on ஒழுக்கு, which can mean a flow or conduct. On the second reading, the chapter ends by saying morality depends on rain.

positions.position: ஒழுக்கு is the unceasing flow of water, and he records the conduct reading as someone else's.
positions.quote: அந்நீர் இடையறாது ஒழுகும் ஒழுக்கும் வானை இன்றி அமையாது.

positions.position: ஒழுக்கு is conduct, which may decay if there is no rain.

links.note: In 1031, the whole world follows the plough. This verse adds what the praise of agriculture leaves out: the plough itself follows the rain.
Here giving and austerity cannot last without rain. In 34, virtue is simply a spotless mind and everything else is noise. If virtue is only inward, the drought in 19 shouldn't threaten it.
Hunger is here the world's worst consequence of drought, a natural evil. In 225, relieving hunger outranks the ascetic's power to endure it, which turns this natural fact into a moral priority.

source_issues: Kalaignar's entry for verse 17 ends with an unrelated sentence beginning 'இ. அடைநலம் அடைமொழிகளைச்', apparently from a different text. It is not part of his comment on this verse.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 16 and 20.
